1:
The three grounds the tribes plead are read alike by all who count them, each adding a turn. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) numbers them plainly: David was their own countryman, he had been their general under Saul and had always led them to victory, and God had appointed him. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) presses the first into a mutual claim — not only art thou our bone and flesh, but we are thine, and thou hast as tender a concern for us as a man has for his own body, which Saul’s house had not — and sharpens the second, that when Saul was king he was but the cypher and David the figure. On the third he glosses the shepherd language: princes are to feed their people, consulting the subjects’ benefit, feeding them and not fleecing them. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) takes the same word as an admonition, that David was not made king to advance his own glory but for the good of his people.

Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) alone notices that the divine promise they quote is nowhere on record. The exact language is not found in the history, and he offers two accounts: either a summary of communications made to David, as with words given earlier to Abner, or some unrecorded saying of a prophet. He also enlarges the assembly from the elders to the great bodies of warriors listed in Chronicles, observes that the men of Judah, over whom David was already king, joined it, and notes the Levites present under Jehoiada, with Zadok appearing only as a conspicuous member of that family. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) take the elders as the more exact definition of the tribes, and add that Chronicles supplies the words according to the word of the Lord through Samuel, so that the old command to anoint David found its complete fulfilment here. John Gill (reformed) has the tribes send ambassadors first, who report their reception, after which the elders come.

What the league was is answered with care. Ellicott warns that it would be an anachronism to read it as a constitutional monarchy, but allows that it may have covered particular matters — leading them against their enemies, sparing the remnant of Saul’s house, and not showing the partiality Saul had shown to men of his own tribe. Wesley puts it as mutual obligation, David to rule by God’s laws and the people to obey. Henry calls the terms sworn and subscribed on both sides, David binding himself to protect them as judge in peace and captain in war, and makes the witness the point, that it was a league before the Lord. Clarke marks it as the third anointing, David having now taken the whole kingdom; and Henry draws from the three stages that his advances were gradual, so that his faith might be tried and experience gained, his kingdom thus typifying a greater one that was to come to its height by degrees.

The thirty years are made to carry chronology and typology at once. Henry notes that at thirty the Levites were first appointed to begin their administration, that about that age the Son of David entered on his public ministry, and that then men come to their full maturity of judgment. Gill makes the same comparison and reckons from the seven and a half years at Hebron that David was near thirty-eight when the elders came to him. Ellicott works outward from the figure: it sets the combat with Goliath some ten or twelve years back, proves that the greater part of Saul’s reign is treated very briefly, and makes David seventy at his death. On the odd six months he observes that the sacred historians either dropped such fractions or counted them as whole years, an indefiniteness very marked in the parallel narratives of the two kingdoms.
6:
What the Jebusites meant by the blind and the lame is the chapter’s hardest crux. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) offers two answers and prefers neither outright: either they confided in their gods, which David in contempt called the blind and the lame, for they have eyes and see not, feet and walk not — some thinking these were images of brass set in a recess of the fort and entrusted with its custody, idols they called their strongholds — or else in fortifications they thought so impregnable that the maimed could hold them. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) takes only the second, supposing they set a parcel of blind and lame people, invalids or maimed soldiers, on the wall in contempt of David and his men. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) corrects the rendering to Thou shalt not come hither, but the blind and the lame shall keep thee off, making it a boast rather than a condition; and Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) ground the boast in the site, a mountain shut in by deep valleys on three sides.

Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) declines the dispute and then supplies an emendation anyway. Scarcely a passage in the sacred oracles, he says, has puzzled commentators more; for his own part he thinks it not worth the labour spent on it, and will not encumber his pages with the discordant opinions of learned men. On the face of the text, he says, the Jebusites simply set the lame and blind on the walls to turn David’s attempt into ridicule, than which nothing could be more cutting to a warrior. He then prints Kennicott’s corrected text beside the English, which turns the taunt into a prediction that the blind and the lame shall drive David away, and promises the chief command to whoever reaches them through the subterranean passage.

That promise is where Ellicott finds the most. The word rendered gutter occurs elsewhere only once, as waterspouts, and likeliest means the watercourses about the precipices of Zion; a very slight change in the Masoretic vowels turns getteth into hurl, so that the order reads, whosoever smites the Jebusites, let him hurl the lame and the blind down the precipice, David throwing their phrase back at them. That they are hated of his soul shows no quarter was to be given, these Canaanites lying under the old ban. The words he shall be chief and captain are not in the Hebrew here, but Chronicles has them, and from them Ellicott draws a consequence no one else does: David promised the command of his army to whoever led the forlorn hope, Joab did it, and that helps explain the restraint David afterwards felt towards him. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same rendering, and Wesley keeps the older one of scaling to the gutter at the top, noting that the missing clause is fitly supplied from Chronicles.

Two accounts are given of how the saying became a proverb. Henry has the Jebusites say it first, meaning that if their images could not protect them they would never again trust their palladium, and David, having taken the fort, said it after them, that images which could not protect their worshippers should have no place there more. Wesley makes it David’s own, ordained to keep up the memory of the exploit and of the Jebusites’ insolence, so that those once set to keep others out are now shut out themselves. On the settlement that followed, Keil and Delitzsch derive Zion from a root meaning dry and explain the choice of it as naturally strong and conveniently placed on the border of Benjamin and Judah; John Gill (reformed) notes that David could not attempt a city partly Benjamin’s until that tribe had made him king; and Henry, watching him prosper from Millo inward, ascribes such greatness to God’s presence.
11:
Whether this Hiram is Solomon’s is disputed outright. John Gill (reformed) makes him the father of that one, named Abibalus before he took the name Hiram, which became a common name of Tyre’s kings, and dates the city to a year before the fall of Troy. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) holds him the same man and works out the cost: since that Hiram was still living in the twenty-fourth year of Solomon’s reign, either he reigned some fifty-seven years or this embassy came well after the capture of Jerusalem. He rejects the thirty-four years Josephus quotes from Menander, since David was already in his house of cedar, before Solomon was born, when he purposed to build the temple — though he grants the later Huram’s father bore the same name. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) treat him simply as the ally of both kings, and Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) calls him a very friendly man and no doubt a believer in the true God.

That foreigners built the palace is noticed by two, to opposite effect. Ellicott infers a want of skill: the Israelites evidently had little architecture of their own, relying on the Phoenicians for this palace, for Solomon’s, and for the temple. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) grants the fact — the Jews were husbandmen and shepherds and did not much addict themselves to merchandise or manufactures — but turns it: many have excelled in arts and sciences who were strangers to the covenants of promise, and David’s house was never the worse, nor the less fit to be dedicated to God, for being built by the sons of the stranger.

On David’s perceiving why he was established, all six converge and Henry draws it out furthest. His kingdom was established with nothing to shake it, and exalted in the eyes of friends and enemies alike; and he perceived it, which Henry makes the heart of the verse — many have God’s favour and do not perceive it, and so want the comfort of it, but to be exalted to it, established in it, and to perceive it, is happiness enough. Above all he owned the reason: God did not make Israel his subjects for his sake, that he might be great and absolute, but made him their king for their sake, to lead and guide and protect them. Ellicott puts it as self-knowledge, that prosperity had not blinded David to his blessings coming to him as head of the theocracy; John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) that he might be a blessing to them; Keil and Delitzsch that God had chosen Israel and promised to make it great; and Gill that David read it off his unbroken success.

The wives are condemned by every voice, and the accounts of the motive differ. Henry is blunt: shall we praise him for this? We praise him not, we justify him not, nor can we scarcely excuse him — though the patriarchs’ example might make him think there was no harm in it, and he might hope it would strengthen his interest by alliances. Wesley reckons it among David’s miscarriages, expressly forbidden to a king, and assigns the same political motive; both add, in almost the same words, that all these wives did not keep him from coveting his neighbour’s, since men who have once broken the fence will wander. Keil and Delitzsch make it cultural capture, a large harem having been held from time immemorial part of an oriental court, so that David let custom seduce him past the prohibition. Ellicott says he came perilously near a violation without going the length of Solomon. Clarke alone argues from nature: that dispensation permitted polygamy, but from the beginning it was not so, and since on average about fourteen males are born to thirteen females, polygamy is unnatural and could never have entered God’s original design.
17:
Why the Philistines moved when they did is answered alike by four voices. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) observes that since Saul fell they had held the principal places of Israel undisturbed, and now thought best to strike before David’s army grew too numerous. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) adds that their attention had been occupied with Abner and Ishbosheth, so that only the uniting of the old nation under their old foe alarmed them — and that the time their mustering took is what allowed David to take Jerusalem first. John Gill (reformed) lists the provocations together — the civil war ended, David strengthened, Jerusalem taken, Hiram befriended — and reports Kimchi’s view that David wrote the second psalm then. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) reaches that psalm independently, the heathen raging in vain. He puts their calculation sharply — he that under Saul had slain his ten thousands, what would he do now he was king? — and their error more sharply, that they considered not how David had the presence of God which Saul had forfeited.

That David enquired twice is made much of, and for different reasons. Henry divides the question: his conscience asked whether he should go up, his prudence whether he would prosper. One would think the first needed no asking, since what was he made king for but to fight the Lord’s battles; but a good man loves to see God go before him. And Henry alone finds a scruple in it, that though the Philistines were public enemies some had been his particular friends, Achish having sheltered him in his distress — ought he not, remembering that, rather to make peace? The answer is that they are Israel’s enemies, and he need not scruple. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) use the two enquiries polemically, as overthrowing Diestel’s assertion that the holy lot is not heard of after Saul’s death, and with it his inference that David valued it only to give definiteness to his command over his followers rather than from reverence. Gill notes that having prospered once he still would not engage again without the mind of God.

The first victory is read through the gods the Philistines abandoned. Gill, Clarke and Ellicott agree they had brought them to the field as Israel once brought the ark, and that leaving them shows how sudden the rout was; Keil and Delitzsch add that Chronicles supplies the burning, which the law prescribed. Henry closes it with Bishop Patrick’s antithesis: when the ark fell into Philistine hands it consumed them, but when these images fell into the hands of Israel they could not save themselves from being consumed — a sentence John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) gives almost word for word, without naming its author.

The trees and the sound in them divide everyone. Keil and Delitzsch refuse both traditional renderings, the Greek pear-trees and the rabbinic mulberries, as uncertain, and prefer an Arabic shrub of Mecca like the balsam, from a broken leaf of which flows a white sap like a tear — whence, they suppose, its name, from the root meaning to weep. Ellicott takes the same shrub as now generally understood, and notes that the word for the sound is used elsewhere of the Lord’s hosts marching. On what the sound was, Gill has the wind rustling the tops so as to resemble armies moving in the air, and reports that Jarchi and the Targum take it for angels sent to help David; Henry allows that angels tread light, and that he who can walk on the clouds can walk on the tops of trees, though he gives Bishop Patrick’s reading of the phrase as the hedge-row of the wood. Wesley makes it work both ways, assuring David that God was coming and frightening the Philistines so that they never heard his army until it was upon them.
